activities.anchor: Many firms create value they never capture
activities.caption: drag the divider — two halves, two skills
activities.name: wbCreateCompare

config.prompt: Creating value vs capturing value — drag the divider across the card:

before.label: creating value
before.text: Making something worth more to a customer than the inputs cost. Newspapers after the internet created enormous value — informing a nation — and captured almost none of it.

after.label: capturing value
after.text: Keeping part of the surplus as price above cost. Others capture value they never created — rents, lock-ins, tricks — until customers find the exit.

config.why: Most business failure is one of the two halves missing — and the value you capture depends less on how much you create than on how hard you are to replace.

activities.caption: call the added value per cup
activities.name: wbCafeEstimate

config.prompt: The café pays 1.20 for beans, milk and labour and sells the cup for 3.50. What is the added value per cup?
config.why: 2.30 — and it pays for the rent, the risk and the owner's living, because a convenient hot cappuccino at 8 a.m. is worth more to the customer than 3.50.
config.context: Value is defined by the customer's willingness to pay, not the producer's cost or pride.

config.prompt: Primary, secondary or tertiary? File each:
config.why: The classification is history: by 2023 agriculture employs under 1.5 per cent of UK workers and services over 80 per cent — the standard drift of rich economies.

activities.anchor: Mergers come in three named flavours
activities.caption: pair each merger with its motive
activities.name: wbMergerMatch

config.prompt: Three growth-by-merger flavours — pair each with its motive:

pairs.right: two competitors combine — instant market share, instant regulator scrutiny
buy a supplier or distributor — control of the chain, not share of a market
unrelated businesses under one roof — pure diversification, now out of fashion

config.why: Backward integration reaches toward raw materials, forward toward the customer — and investors can diversify themselves more cheaply than a conglomerate can.

activities.anchor: The failures have a short, repeated list of causes
activities.caption: one line of the failure checklist is wrong
activities.name: wbFailureSpot

config.prompt: One line of this failure-checklist summary is wrong. Find it.
lines: Roughly half of new businesses are gone within five years
Lack of cash leads the list — profitable on paper, dead in practice
Over-expansion grows faster than working capital and management can carry
Most of the causes are inflicted by competitors and bad luck
Key-person dependence routes everything through one founder's head
config.correction: Four of the five are self-inflicted — cash, no market, over-expansion, key-person dependence.
config.why: Which is why 'survival' appears first in nearly every list of business objectives, and why seasoned operators respect boring cash discipline more than exciting strategy.

activities.anchor: profitable on paper and dead in practice
activities.caption: true or false — profit versus the calendar
activities.name: wbProfitJudge

statements.why: Profit is an accounting verdict over a period; suppliers, wages and rent fall due on dates.

statements.s: A firm that collects from customers sixty days after paying its own suppliers can be profitable on paper and dead in practice.
statements.why: That timing gap is why 'lack of cash' leads the list of killers.

statements.s: Over-expansion is the classic way good restaurants die on opening their third branch.
statements.why: Growing faster than working capital and management can carry.

statements.s: 'No market' means the firm built something because it could be built.
statements.why: Second on the checklist — value defined by the producer, not the customer.

activities.anchor: Legal form is a choice with consequences
activities.caption: pick the legal skin, own the consequences
activities.name: wbFormBranch

config.root: Three founders, three appetites for risk, control and capital. Choose each legal form.

start.text: Founder one wants trivial setup and total control, and will sign for the debts personally. The form?

choices.label: Sole trader
choices.feedback: Unlimited liability — the business's debts are recoverable from the house and savings.

choices.label: Company
choices.feedback: Safer but heavier — more form than a one-person gamble needs.

sole.text: Founder two joins — pooled capital and skill, but the liability question stays. What now?

choices.label: General partnership — share everything, liability included
choices.feedback: General partners share unlimited liability — which is why formal agreements and limited partners exist.

choices.label: Incorporate as a company
choices.feedback: The separate legal person owns its own debts — shareholders lose only what they invested.

company.text: Founder three needs vast capital from strangers. What unlocks it?

choices.label: Public limited company — freely traded shares
choices.feedback: Vast capital, at the price of listing requirements and answering to the stock market every quarter.

choices.label: Stay private — shares by invitation only
choices.feedback: Suits family and founder-owned firms — capital stays scarcer.

partner.text: Capital pooled, risk shared — and the agreement on paper while everyone still likes each other.

plc.text: Since the Dutch East India Company's 1602 public share issue, this is the machine that funds huge risky ventures.

ltd.text: Private and patient — control kept, growth slower.

config.why: Limited liability — shareholders lose only what they invested, never their homes — is what made modern capital markets possible.

activities.anchor: Cross-cutting all of the legal forms is a quieter design choice
activities.caption: file each revenue model by its obsession
activities.name: wbRevenueBuckets

config.prompt: Choose the revenue model, inherit its incentives. File each obsession:

items.label: retention and churn — a 10-a-month subscriber staying 30 months is a 300 customer
the user is the audience being assembled and sold
a 2–5 per cent converting minority subsidises a large free majority

config.why: A subscription newspaper investigates its government differently from an advertising-funded one — the model shapes behaviour more decisively than the legal form.
